Optimal number of clusters: Elbow method (WSS)

Source: R/seg_prep.R
seg_nbclust_wss.Rd

Computes the total within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) for 1 to k_max clusters using factoextra::fviz_nbclust(). The optimal number of clusters is located at the "elbow" (bend) of the curve, where adding another cluster no longer reduces the WSS much.

Usage

seg_nbclust_wss(
  x,
  cluster_method = c("kmeans", "hclust", "pam"),
  k_max = 10,
  nstart = 25,
  hc_method = "ward.D2",
  seed = 123
)

Arguments

x

The output of seg_prep_data() (recommended), or a data frame or numeric matrix with already prepared clustering variables (no missing values).

cluster_method

Clustering algorithm used to evaluate the solutions: "kmeans" (default, stats::kmeans()), "hclust" (hierarchical clustering via factoextra::hcut()) or "pam" (partitioning around medoids, cluster::pam()). k-means always uses Euclidean distances. NbClust does not support "pam" and is skipped in that case.

k_max

Maximum number of clusters to consider. Defaults to 10.

nstart

Number of random starts for k-means (WSS, silhouette). Defaults to 25.

hc_method

Agglomeration method for cluster_method = "hclust". Defaults to "ward.D2".

seed

Random seed. The global random seed is left untouched. Defaults to 123.

Value

A list with the elements method, optimal_k, criterion, values (tibble with the criterion per k) and plot (ggplot object).

Details

How it works

For each k, the respondents are clustered and the total within-cluster sum of squares is computed: $$WSS(k) = \sum_{c=1}^{k} \sum_{i \in C_c} d(x_i, \mu_c)^2$$ where \(\mu_c\) is the center of cluster \(c\). WSS measures the compactness of the clusters: the smaller, the more similar the respondents within the clusters. If a distance matrix other than Euclidean was computed by seg_prep_data(), it is used to compute the WSS.

Since WSS always decreases when clusters are added (with k = n respondents it is 0), its minimum is meaningless. Instead, the elbow method looks for the k after which adding clusters brings only small improvements. Here, the elbow is determined automatically as the point with the largest distance below the straight line between the first and the last point of the (normalized) curve.

Interpretation

  • A sharp bend indicates a natural number of clusters.

  • A smooth curve without a clear bend, which is common for survey data, indicates that the data has no clear cluster structure. The automatically determined elbow is then only a rough guide and may change with k_max.

  • The elbow method is the most widely used but also the most subjective method. Combine it with the other methods of seg_optimal_clusters().

See also

Other optimal number of clusters: seg_nbclust_gap(), seg_nbclust_indices(), seg_nbclust_silhouette()

Examples

# \donttest{
prep <- seg_prep_data(iris, vars = -Species, verbose = FALSE)
seg_nbclust_wss(prep)$plot

# }
